note: Cited to pinned Wikipedia revisions (trusted_secondary): East African Rift and Great Rift Valley. Figures are quoted as the pages state them. The future separation of eastern Africa is only the page's attributed projection (marine geologist Kathleen Crane, 'could eventually', 'tens of millions of years'); no sea, coastline or plate boundary is drawn, because the map data holds none and a drawn one would be invented geometry. The Rutanzige lake the page lists in the western branch is not used as a map place. Lakes are the registry's lake outlines. Lake Turkana is the page's northernmost part of the eastern branch (with the Omo valley); the frames that show it also show, unlabelled, the Natural Earth lines around the Ilemi Triangle (flagged for review on Kenya) because the lake lies just south of it, so the subject and regions avoid Kenya, Sudan and Somalia. BORDERS: no place named here carries a review flag; a person should still glance at the wide frames, which show unlabelled country lines across East Africa.

claims.text: The East African Rift is an active continental rift zone and a developing divergent tectonic plate boundary where the African plate is in the process of splitting into two tectonic plates, called the Somali plate and the Nubian plate, at a rate of 8–9 mm per year.
The East African Rift began developing around the onset of the Miocene, 22–25 million years ago.

Southward from the Afar triple junction, the East African Rift consists of two main branches: the Eastern Rift Valley (Gregory Rift), which runs through Ethiopia and Kenya into northern Tanzania, and the Western Rift Valley, which includes the Albertine Rift and transects the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, and farther south Tanzania, Zambia, the valley of Lake Malawi and Mozambique.
Many of the African Great Lakes lie within the Rift Valley.
The western branch of the Great Rift Valley consists mainly of a series of deep lakes: Lake Albert, Lake Rutanzige, Lake Kivu, Lake Tanganyika and Lake Rukwa.
Lake Tanganyika is the second largest and second deepest freshwater lake in the world.
The northernmost part of the eastern branch is formed by the valley of the Omo river in southern Ethiopia and Lake Turkana in Kenya.
The southernmost section of the Great Rift Valley includes Lake Malawi, the third-deepest freshwater body in the world, which reaches 706 metres in depth.
According to marine geologist Kathleen Crane, the rift could eventually cause eastern Africa to separate from the mainland, although this potential event could take tens of millions of years.
The East African Rift is the largest seismically active rift system on Earth today.
